questions.question: Doxycycline MOA

parts.text: What is the mechanism of action of Doxycycline?
What substance or medication that when taken with Doxycycline reduces its efficacy AND why?
Complete this table regarding duration of doxycycline for: Community Acquired Pneumonia; Chlamydia urethritis; LGV
How would you counsel someone to take Doxycycline as post-exposure prophylaxis for prevention of STI?

questions.model_answer:
a) Mechanism of action: reversibly binds the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, blocking aminoacyl-tRNA binding to the ribosomal acceptor (A) site, preventing peptide chain elongation and inhibiting protein synthesis (bacteriostatic).
b) Reduced efficacy with concurrent multivalent cations (calcium, magnesium, iron, aluminum) — found in antacids, dairy products, and iron/mineral supplements — because these cations chelate doxycycline in the gut, reducing its absorption by 50-90%; separating administration by about 3 hours prevents this interaction.
c) Duration table: Community-acquired pneumonia — doxycycline 100 mg PO/IV BID, typically 5-7 days; Chlamydia urethritis (uncomplicated genital C. trachomatis) — 100 mg PO BID x 7 days; Lymphogranuloma venereum — 100 mg PO BID x 21 days.
d) DoxyPEP counseling: take a single dose of doxycycline 200 mg by mouth as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours (and no later than 72 hours) after condomless oral, vaginal, or anal sex, as post-exposure prophylaxis to reduce risk of chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis; not for use more than once per day even with multiple exposures.
questions.cites: Mandell pp. 322, 329, 331-332 (CAP duration and DoxyPEP counseling from general/CDC guidance, not explicit in this chapter)
questions.beyond_mandell: DoxyPEP dosing/counseling reflects the 2024 CDC doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis guidance, not covered in this Mandell chapter; CAP duration reflects general ATS/IDSA CAP guideline practice (chapter gives dosing for legionellosis/atypicals but not a specific CAP course length).

parts.text: Are the following bacteria generally susceptible to Tigecycline and if no, what is the mechanism of resistance? Pseudomonas; Acinetobacter; Morganella; VRE

cohort_answer.text: Pseudomonas - no, multidrug efflux pump. Acinetobacter - yes. Morganella - no, multidrug efflux pump (AcrAB). VRE - yes (only Vanco susceptible E. faecalis). MOA: glycylcycline; binds bacterial 30S ribosome, blocks tRNA entry, prevents protein synthesis limiting bacterial growth.

a) PK: less frequent (BID) dosing, no renal/HD adjustment needed. PD: coverage of AROs incl MRSA, VRE, ESBL, AmpCs, CRE, atypicals, NTM, Nocardia. b) Pseudomonas; Proteus mirabilis; Providencia; Morganella.

questions.question: AM 11. List of paired antimicrobials (from a to j) asked which you would choose for. (3 - 0.5 each). Options: Valganciclovir over acyclovir; Famciclovir over acyclovir; Doxycycline over Septra; Metronidazole over clindamycin; Piptazo over meropenem; Ampicillin over cloxacillin; Cefuroxime over CTX; Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin; Fluconazole over caspofungin; Atovaquone over dapsone

parts.text: a. I would pick __ over ___ because patient on tegretol
b. I would pick _____ over _____ because patient has G6PD deficiency
c. I would pick ___ over _____ because drug not used for cdiff treatment and not associated with development of cdiff
d. I would pick _____ over _____ because it has superior renal penetration
e. I would pick _____ over _____ because it works better for CMV
f. I would pick _____ over _____ because it works better for a bacteria in the CNS

cohort_answer.text: a) Pip/Tazo over Mero because patient on tegretol. b) Atovaquone over Dapsone because patient has G6PD deficiency. c) Doxycycline over Septra because drug not used for CDI treatment and not associated with development of CDI. d) Fluconazole over Caspofungin because it has superior renal penetration. e) Valganciclovir over acyclovir because it works better for CMV. f) Moxifloxacin over Levofloxacin because it works better for a bacteria in the CNS.

parts.text: Name three antibiotics with gram negative coverage that are intrinsically resistant to proteus and providencia

questions.model_answer: 3 gram-negative-active urinary agents intrinsically inactive against Proteus and Providencia: (1) nitrofurantoin, (2) fosfomycin, (3) polymyxin B/colistin.

parts.text: List 5 non-beta-lactams with excellent bioavailability. Only use each class once.

questions.model_answer: 5 non-beta-lactam classes with excellent oral bioavailability: (1) fluoroquinolones, (2) metronidazole, (3) trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, (4) tetracyclines (e.g., doxycycline), (5) oxazolidinones (linezolid).
